# `js/prefer-set-has`

**A `Set` for a list that is only searched**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pack** | `@codelaw/rules-js` (npm) · `codelaw-rules-js` (PyPI) |
| **Languages** | JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX |
| **Turned on by** | `codelaw:js/strict` at `error` |
| **Severity when named without one** | `error` |
| **Options** | `minimumItems` |
| **Fix** | `auto` — `codelaw fix` applies it; it never changes what the code does |
| **Stability** | `preview` — runs only with `preview = true` |
| **Since** | 0.5.0 |
| **Ported from** | `eslint-plugin-unicorn/prefer-set-has` |

## What it checks

A variable initialised with an array (a literal, `Array()`, `Array.from()`/`Array.of()`, or a method that returns a new array: `map`, `filter`, `split`, …) whose every use is `x.includes(value)` is reported at its name. A single `includes()` counts only when it runs repeatedly — in a loop or a function below the declaration. For a literal of unique primitives, `x.length`, `for…of`, spreading and `forEach` with one parameter may be used too. The fix wraps the value in `new Set(…)`, renames `includes` to `has` and `length` to `size`, and turns a `T[]` or `Array<T>` annotation into `Set<T>` (another annotation makes it a suggestion). An exported or reassigned variable is left alone.

**Why:** `includes()` scans the whole array each time; `Set.has()` is a lookup.

## Configuration

Everything below goes in `codelaw.toml` at the repo root. The same keys work as `[tool.codelaw]` in `pyproject.toml` or `"codelaw"` in `package.json` ([SR-CONFIG](../../../records/0110_config.md)).

### Turn it on

**Install the pack** (`codelaw init` does it for the languages it finds):

```bash
npm install --save-dev @codelaw/rules-js
pip install codelaw-rules-js
```

**Then extend a preset that turns it on** — `codelaw:js/strict` sets it to `error`:

```toml
preview = true                        # pack rules are preview today
extends = ["codelaw:js/strict"]
```

- **A rule exists only once its pack is loaded** through `extends`; naming it in `[rules]` without that is an unknown rule id (exit 2).
- **Without `preview = true`** the rule is skipped and codelaw warns that it is preview.

### Severity

```toml
[rules]
"js/prefer-set-has" = "warn"    # error | warn | info | off
```

- **`error`** fails the run (exit 1) · **`warn`** fails only with `--max-warnings N` · **`info`** never fails · **`off`** turns it off.
- **Naming it with a severity turns it on** even when no preset does.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `minimumItems` | `integer` | `0` | report only arrays known to hold at least this many items; 0 reports any size |

**Every option at its default** — a starting point to copy:

```toml
[rules."js/prefer-set-has"]
severity = "error"

[rules."js/prefer-set-has".options]
minimumItems = 0
```

**The same, inline, with example values:**

```toml
[rules]
"js/prefer-set-has" = { severity = "error", options = { minimumItems = 3 } }
```

- **A table without `severity`** changes only the options: the severity stays what a preset or an earlier layer set, and a rule that is off stays off.
- **A list option replaces its default** — copy the default entries you want to keep.
- **An unknown option or a value of the wrong type** stops the run with exit 2 and names the nearest option.

#### `minimumItems`

*integer* · default `0`

report only arrays known to hold at least this many items; 0 reports any size

```toml
[rules."js/prefer-set-has".options]
minimumItems = 3
```

### Options in action

Each case below is one of the rule's tests (`packs/js/rules/js/prefer-set-has.cases.md`): the options, the input, and what codelaw reports.

#### minimum items

```toml
[rules."js/prefer-set-has".options]
minimumItems = 3
```

```js
const xs = [1, 2];
const f = (v) => xs.includes(v);
```

**Reports nothing.**

### For a group of files

A `[scope.<name>]` gives some files their own setting, applied after `[rules]` — the `tests` scope `codelaw:js/recommended` ships (`**/*.test.*`, `**/*.spec.*`); naming it extends it, so its files stay:

```toml
[scope.tests]
rules = { "js/prefer-set-has" = { options = { minimumItems = 3 } } }
```

Or switch it off there:

```toml
[scope.tests]
rules = { "js/prefer-set-has" = "off" }
```

A scope's `remap` changes whole severities in its files, after everything else: `remap = { error = "warn" }` never fails the run there.

### Warn locally, fail in CI

The `ci` profile runs when `CI` is set; `local` otherwise; `--profile <name>` or `CODELAW_PROFILE` picks one.

```toml
[profile.local.rules]
"js/prefer-set-has" = "warn"

[profile.ci.rules]
"js/prefer-set-has" = "error"
```

### In `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.codelaw.rules]
"js/prefer-set-has" = { severity = "warn", options = { minimumItems = 3 } }
```

```json
{
  "codelaw": {
    "rules": {
      "js/prefer-set-has": {"severity": "warn", "options": {"minimumItems": 3}}
    }
  }
}
```

### Silence one finding

An inline `codelaw-ignore` always needs a reason; `expires=`, `warn_days=` and `by=` date it ([SR-LINTER](../../../records/0106_linter.md) decision 6).

- **JavaScript:** `// codelaw-ignore js/prefer-set-has: <reason>`
- **Dated:** `// codelaw-ignore js/prefer-set-has expires=2026-12-31 by=you@example.com: <reason>`

### Keep today's findings, fail on new ones

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule js/prefer-set-has --expires 2026-12-31 --reason "<why>"
```

See [SR-BASELINE](../../../records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md).

### See what applies

```bash
codelaw explain js/prefer-set-has       # what it wants, why, how to fix
codelaw check --rule js/prefer-set-has  # only this rule
codelaw config --print --for <file>     # the resolved setting, and where it came from
```

## Examples

### JavaScript

#### Don't

```js
const allowed = ["a", "b"];
const ok = (v) => allowed.includes(v);
```

#### Do

```js
const allowed = new Set(["a", "b"]);
const ok = (v) => allowed.has(v);
```

#### Fixed

```js
const allowed = new Set(["a", "b"]);
const ok = (v) => allowed.has(v);
```
